examples.file: 01 The Keeling curve with seasonal decomposition.kclim
examples.title: The Keeling curve with seasonal decomposition
examples.description: Atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa since 1958 split into a long-term trend (quadratic), the seasonal cycle (four harmonics) and the residual. The cycle peaks in May and bottoms out in October as the northern forests grow and rot.

examples.title: CO₂ seasonal amplitude is growing
examples.description: The size of the Mauna Loa seasonal cycle, year by year (a harmonic fit in a sliding 5-year window), with its trend and 95 % confidence band. More CO₂ and a longer growing season make the northern-hemisphere breathing deeper.

examples.title: Warming stripes 1850–now (HadCRUT5)
examples.description: One stripe per year, blue for cooler and red for warmer than the 1961–1990 average, in the style of Ed Hawkins. Nothing else: no axes, no numbers, just the pattern of the last 175 years.

examples.title: Warming stripes 1880–now (GISTEMP)
examples.description: The same picture from NASA’s GISTEMP record, which starts in 1880. Compare with the HadCRUT5 stripes: two independent analyses of the same thermometers and ships tell the same story.

examples.file: 05 Global warming trend per decade, with confidence band.kclim
examples.title: Global warming trend per decade, with confidence band
examples.description: A straight line through the annual GISTEMP anomalies since 1970 gives about 0.2 °C per decade. The interval allows for the autocorrelation of the residuals (AR(1)), which is wider than the textbook one.

examples.file: 06 Is warming accelerating - a breakpoint and three periods.kclim
examples.title: Is warming accelerating: a breakpoint and three periods
examples.description: A two-segment trend fitted to GISTEMP since 1880 finds a break in the 1970s, after which warming is several times faster. The period comparison shows the trend per decade of three eras with their confidence intervals.

examples.title: Baselines: 1951–1980 vs 1961–1990 vs pre-industrial
examples.description: The same HadCRUT5 record expressed against three baselines. The curves have identical shape and differ only by a constant: the choice of baseline moves the zero line, not the warming.

examples.file: 08 ENSO and global temperature - lagged correlation.kclim
examples.title: ENSO and global temperature: lagged correlation
examples.description: Cross-correlation of the Oceanic Niño Index with GISTEMP monthly anomalies, both detrended: global temperature follows El Niño by about three months.

examples.file: 09 Observed warming vs CO2, ENSO and volcanoes (regression).kclim
examples.title: Observed warming vs CO₂, ENSO and volcanoes (regression)
examples.description: Monthly GISTEMP regressed on log₂(CO₂), the ENSO index (3 months earlier) and volcanic aerosol (4 months earlier), 1960–2012. The CO₂ coefficient is the warming per doubling; the green curve has the natural wiggles taken out.

examples.file: 10 September Arctic sea-ice decline and trend.kclim
examples.title: September Arctic sea-ice decline and trend
examples.description: The Arctic sea-ice extent at its yearly minimum (September), 1979 to now, with a linear trend of about −0.7 million km² per decade and its confidence interval.

examples.file: 11 Sea level - tide gauges and satellites.kclim
examples.title: Sea level: tide gauges and satellites
examples.description: Global mean sea level from the CSIRO tide-gauge reconstruction (1880–2013) and NOAA satellite altimetry (1993–now), both zeroed on 1993–2013 so that they can be compared. Rising ever faster.

examples.file: 12 Doubling CO2 - 1.1 K with no feedbacks, 3 K with them.kclim
examples.title: Doubling CO₂: 1.1 K with no feedbacks, 3 K with them
examples.description: CO₂ is doubled at once in a zero-dimensional energy-balance model. The planet warms until outgoing radiation balances the extra 3.7 W/m²: by 1.1 K without feedbacks, by 3 K with the net feedback of a climate sensitivity of 3 K per doubling.

examples.title: Net zero by 2050 (toy scenario)
examples.description: Emissions fall in a straight line from today’s level to zero in 2050. The model starts from the real emission history and Mauna Loa CO₂, and warming above 1850–1900 is compared with observed HadCRUT5. A teaching model, not a projection.

examples.file: 14 Business as usual - emissions growing 1 % a year (toy scenario).kclim
examples.title: Business as usual: emissions growing 1 % a year (toy scenario)
examples.description: Same model, but emissions keep growing by 1 % a year from 2025. Compare the end-of-century warming with the net-zero example.

examples.file: 15 Ice-albedo bistability and the snowball hysteresis loop.kclim
examples.title: Ice–albedo bistability and the snowball hysteresis loop
examples.description: When ice reflects more sunlight, a cooler Earth gets colder still. With that feedback the same sunlight allows two stable climates, and sweeping the solar constant down and back up traces a hysteresis loop: a frozen Earth needs far more sunlight to thaw than it took to freeze.

examples.file: 16 The 255 K Earth with no greenhouse effect.kclim
examples.title: The 255 K Earth with no greenhouse effect
examples.description: Without an atmosphere that absorbs infrared, Earth’s surface would settle at 255 K (−18 °C): the temperature at which it radiates away the sunlight it absorbs. The real 288 K is 33 K warmer, and that difference is the natural greenhouse effect.

examples.file: 17 Import your own CSV - a synthetic weather station.kclim
examples.title: Import your own CSV: a synthetic weather station
examples.description: A starter for your own time series: a made-up weather station (synthetic data, not observations) imported as monthly temperature and rainfall. Use File › Import CSV… with your own file: choose the time column and the value columns, and everything in kClimate works on it.
